rationale: The student added both numerators and denominators (2/5 + 1/5 = 3/10). Using a number line marked in unit fraction increments shows that hopping along fifths increases the count of fifths without changing the denominator/unit size. A different problem with a different sum is chosen (1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5).

script.focus: The size of each hop stays one fifth, so the total count of fifths increases while the denominator remains 5.

intent: Demonstrate add on the number-line with values [1,3] (unit 1/5). Tutor points at: The size of each hop stays one fifth, so the total count of fifths increases while the denominator remains 5.

frames.caption: Start at 1/5. We are standing here; we have not hopped yet.
Hop 1 moves 1/5 forward and lands on 2/5. One hop is one fifth.
Hop 3 lands on 4/5. 3 hops, so 1/5 + 3/5 = 4/5. Every hop was one fifth; the size of the pieces never changed, only how many.

judgement.reasoning: The student mistakenly adds the denominators (getting 3/10 for 2/5 + 1/5). This detour uses a number line demonstration showing hops of size 1/5, explicitly narrating that the hop size (denominator) remains fifths and does not change. Switching from an area model (fraction bar) to a linear measurement model (number line) helps the student see units as fixed sizes rather than counts to combine.
judgement.verdict: Yes, this worked example clearly demonstrates why the denominator remains fifths using an effective alternate representation without spoiling the original question.
